skills.name: Time from GMT and time zones

note.text:
GMT (Greenwich Mean Time) is the time on the Prime Meridian (0°), which passes through Greenwich in London.
Local time from GMT: find the longitude of the place, multiply by 4 minutes, then add for east or subtract for west.
Time zones: 360° ÷ 24 hours gives 24 zones, each about 15° wide. Each zone uses the time of its standard meridian, a multiple of 15°:
• 15°E: GMT+1, 30°E: GMT+2, 45°E: GMT+3 …
• 15°W: GMT−1, 30°W: GMT−2 …
Zone borders often follow country borders, so that a country keeps one time. Very wide countries have several zones.
The International Date Line is near 180°. Crossing it, travellers change the date by one day.
Cameroon, Nigeria, Gabon and Chad use GMT+1.

worked_example.problem: It is {clock(t)} GMT. What is the local time at a place on {lon(L)}?
steps: The place is {abs(L)}° west of Greenwich.

cards.idea: GMT is the time on the Prime Meridian ({lon(0)}) at Greenwich. Times around the world are compared with GMT.
example: {zone(15)} means one hour ahead of GMT.

check.prompt: Where is GMT, Greenwich Mean Time, measured?

right.text: on the Prime Meridian (0°), at Greenwich

wrong.explain: The Equator is a line of latitude; time is measured from the Prime Meridian.
Yaoundé uses GMT+1, one hour ahead of Greenwich.
The Date Line is near 180°, on the other side of the Earth from Greenwich.
GMT is the time on the Prime Meridian at Greenwich.

cards.idea: The world has {24} time zones of about {degreesPerHour()}° each. Each zone uses the time of a standard meridian that is a multiple of {degreesPerHour()}°.
Each {degreesPerHour()}° east of Greenwich is one hour ahead of GMT; each {degreesPerHour()}° west is one hour behind.

questions.prompt: A country uses the standard meridian {lon(m)}. What is its time zone?

misconceptions.explain: East of Greenwich is ahead (+); west is behind (−).
Divide the longitude by 15 to find the number of hours.

questions.prompt: A place uses the time of the meridian {lon(15 * k)}. How many hours ahead of GMT is it?

misconceptions.explain: That is the difference in minutes. Divide the longitude by 15 for hours.

questions.prompt: It is {clock(t)} GMT. What is the time in a country that uses {zone(15 * h)}?

misconceptions.explain: + means ahead of GMT (add); − means behind (subtract).
Only places on GMT have the same time as Greenwich.
Add or subtract exactly the number of hours in the zone name.

questions.prompt: It is {clock(t)} GMT. What is the local time at a place on {lon(L)}?

misconceptions.explain: East of Greenwich is ahead (add); west is behind (subtract).
Each degree is 4 minutes, not 1 minute.
That is the standard time of the nearest zone. Local time uses the exact longitude: 4 minutes for each degree.

questions.prompt: Which sentence about time zones is true?

right.text: Each time zone is about 15° of longitude wide.
There are 24 time zones, one for each hour of the day.
Crossing the International Date Line changes the date.

wrong.explain: 4 is the number of minutes for one degree. A time zone is about 15° wide.

wrong.text: Every country has its own time zone, different from all its neighbours.
wrong.explain: Cameroon, Nigeria, Gabon and Chad all use GMT+1.

wrong.text: The International Date Line is at 0°.
wrong.explain: 0° is the Prime Meridian. The Date Line is near 180°.

wrong.text: Places west of Greenwich are ahead of GMT.
wrong.explain: Places west of Greenwich are behind GMT.

questions.prompt: When the local time at a place on {lon(L)} is {clock(t)}, what time is it at Greenwich (GMT)?

misconceptions.explain: Going from the place back to Greenwich, the direction is reversed: from an eastern place subtract, from a western place add.
Each degree is 4 minutes, not 1 minute.
The place is not on 0°, so its time is different from GMT.

solution: The place is {L > 0 ? 'east' : 'west'} of Greenwich, so Greenwich is {L > 0 ? 'behind: subtract' : 'ahead: add'}. {clock(t)} {L > 0 ? '−' : '+'} {duration(timeForDegrees(abs(L)))} = {answer}
